title: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
summary: Find your way around an unfamiliar repository: map what to skip, search with git grep and GitHub code search, trace a real Redis request, and use blame and pickaxe to learn why code looks the way it does.
outcomes: Explain which files git grep, ripgrep and grep -r search, and pick the right one
Find a definition and its callers with -w, git grep -p and GitHub symbol: search
Trace a request through code that uses function-pointer dispatch, using source and a backtrace
Use git blame -w -M and ignore-revs to see past formatting and move commits
Choose between git log -S, -G and -L to find the commit that introduced or removed code

lessons.title: Map the repository before you read a line of it

blocks.md: You found a bug in a project you use and want to fix it. You clone the repository and face thousands of files written by people you have never met. Reading them top to bottom is hopeless, and it is also unnecessary: a fix usually touches a handful of functions. The skill this course teaches is **navigation**: build a rough map, search to narrow the map to a few files, trace one code path through them, then use version history to learn why the code looks the way it does.

We will use a real codebase throughout: the [Redis](https://github.com/redis/redis) server, a C program. We made a shallow clone (`git clone --depth 1`, only the latest commit) of its default branch and measured it with a script. `git ls-files` lists the **tracked** files, the ones recorded in Git: there are 1,938 of them holding 654,217 lines of text.

blocks.title: Where Redis keeps its 1,938 tracked files

scenes.caption: Share of tracked **files** per top-level directory. The largest group, deps, is not Redis code at all: it is third-party libraries copied into the tree.
Share of **lines** instead. src/commands holds 467 files but only 4.5% of the lines: one small JSON spec per command. The server code in src is 35.3% of all lines.
Drop what you do not need for a server bug: vendored deps and the rest. What remains is src, its specs and the tests. The GET path we trace later lives in just 5 files of src (3.5% of all lines).

blocks.md:
Three questions build the map quickly:

1. **What is not ours?** Vendored code is a copy of another project kept in the tree. Redis says so in `deps/README.md`: the directory "contains all Redis dependencies" (jemalloc, hiredis, lua and others), upgraded from upstream as needed.
2. **What is generated?** Generated files are written by a script and must not be edited by hand.
3. **Where does execution start?** For a server, the `main` function: `git grep -n 'int main' src/server.c` finds it at `src/server.c:8361`.

blocks.code:
# first line of src/commands.def
/* Automatically generated by generate-command-code.py, do not edit. */

# rule in src/Makefile (line 503), Make variables expanded
commands.def: commands/*.json ../utils/generate-command-code.py
	python3 ../utils/generate-command-code.py
blocks.caption: The build file says what is generated from what: commands.def (13,300 lines) is built from the small JSON specs in src/commands by a Python script. Make variables shown expanded (python3, or python if python3 is missing).

blocks.md: A common mistake is to fix a bug inside a generated file. Your edit is overwritten the next time the generator runs, and reviewers will reject it. When a file says *do not edit*, find its input (here `src/commands/get.json`) in the build rule and change that instead.

blocks.title: A reading order for an unfamiliar repository

scenes.caption: Start with the README: what the project is and how to build it. CONTRIBUTING describes how changes are proposed and reviewed.
The build files are a map of the tree: they name generated files, their inputs, and the vendored directories that get built separately.
Find the entry point, then the tests. A test is a precise, runnable statement of expected behavior, often the fastest way to learn what a feature does.

blocks.md: Tests deserve that last step. If you want to know how `GET` behaves on the wrong type of key, `git grep -n WRONGTYPE -- tests` finds assertions such as one in `tests/unit/type/string.tcl` that expects `GETRANGE` on a list key to fail with a WRONGTYPE error. That is a specification written in code, and it is the error we will trace in lesson 3.

blocks.question: You want to change the documented summary of the GET command, which appears in src/commands.def. Which file should your patch edit?
options: src/commands.def, since that is where the text appears
src/commands/get.json, the input the generator reads
src/server.c, since main() loads the command table
blocks.explain: commands.def starts with "Automatically generated ... do not edit", and the Makefile rule shows it is built from commands/*.json by utils/generate-command-code.py. Edit the JSON spec (and regenerate), otherwise the change is lost on the next build.

blocks.question: Your search for a function name returns 40 hits, 30 of them under deps/. What is the best next step for a Redis server bug?
options: Delete deps/ from your clone so search is faster
Restrict the search to src, for example `git grep -n name -- src`, since deps is vendored third-party code
blocks.explain: Vendored code is a copy of another project. Bugs there are usually fixed upstream, not in this repo. A pathspec after `--` limits git grep to the directories that matter without changing the checkout.

lessons.title: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches

blocks.md: Search is how you jump from a name to the few lines that matter. The catch is that each tool decides **which files** to look at before it matches anything. To see the difference, take a tiny Python repository: `src/cache.py` defines `evict`, `src/server.py` and `tests/test_cache.py` call it. Then add two kinds of file Git does not track: `build/`, which is listed in `.gitignore` (an **ignored** file), and `scratch.py`, an experiment that is neither tracked nor ignored (an **untracked** file).

blocks.title: Which files each search tool reads

scenes.caption: `grep -rnw evict .` (with .git excluded) reads every file on disk: 10 matching lines in 6 files. The build copies duplicate every real hit.
`rg -nw evict` (ripgrep) skips files matched by .gitignore, plus hidden and binary files by default. It still reads untracked scratch.py: 7 lines in 4 files.
`git grep -nw evict` searches only tracked files: 5 lines in 3 files. This is exactly the code a reviewer sees in the repository.
`git grep --untracked` adds untracked files (7 lines). Adding `--no-exclude-standard` also reads ignored files, matching grep -r again (10 lines).

blocks.md: The git-grep documentation states the default precisely: it looks for patterns "in the tracked files in the work tree, blobs registered in the index file, or blobs in given tree objects". Ripgrep's guide lists what it skips automatically: .gitignore matches, hidden files and directories, and binary files (any file with a NUL byte). Both are good defaults for reading a project; plain `grep -r` is the one that drowns you in build output and dependency folders.

git grep can also search a version you have not checked out: `git grep -n evict v1.0` searches the tree of tag v1.0. Add a pathspec after `--` to stay inside one directory, for example `git grep -n evict -- src`.

The second filter is the pattern itself. A plain pattern matches inside longer names. In Redis, `lookupKeyRead` is a function, but so are `lookupKeyReadOrReply` and `lookupKeyReadWithFlags`. The `-w` flag (word regexp) only accepts a match that starts and ends at a word boundary, so the longer names no longer count.

scenes.caption: `git grep lookupKeyRead` matches 108 lines in 20 files, because the string also occurs inside longer function names.
`git grep -w lookupKeyRead` keeps whole-word matches only: 55 lines in 15 files.
Classifying the 55 by script: 50 call lines, 3 comment lines, 1 prototype in src/server.h and 1 definition in src/db.c. Only one line tells you what the function does.

blocks.md: Fifty call sites is still a lot of reading. git grep can label each hit with the function it sits in. With `-p` (`--show-function`) it prints "the preceding line that contains the function name of the match", using the same rule as the hunk headers in `git diff`. Every labelled line is a caller.

blocks.caption: Lines with = are function headers, lines with : are matches. Four callers: SET (with its GET option), GET, GETDEL and GETSET. Excerpt of the real output; the prototype and definition lines are omitted.

blocks.prompt: The default header rule picks the nearest earlier line that begins with a letter, an underscore or a dollar sign. A Python file has `class Cache:` on line 1 and an indented method `def drop(self, k):` that calls `self.evict(k)`. What does `git grep -p -w evict` name as the enclosing function?
blocks.reveal: It prints `c.py=1=class Cache:`, the class, not the method, because `    def drop` starts with spaces. We ran it. The fix is to tell Git the language: put `*.py diff=python` in `.gitattributes`, which selects Git's built-in Python pattern. Then the same command prints `c.py=5=    def drop(self, k):`. Git ships built-in patterns for C/C++ (`cpp`), Go (`golang`), Rust (`rust`) and many more.

blocks.md: On GitHub you can do similar searches without cloning. In code search, `repo:redis/redis` limits results to one repository and `path:src` to matching paths, and `symbol:getCommand` finds **definitions** of that name. Symbol search is based on Tree-sitter parsing, so it needs no build. The docs list its limits: it "only searches for definitions and not references", only the default branch is indexed, results stop at 100, and files over 350 KiB are excluded.

GitHub's "find references" is name-based: the docs say it searches all definitions and references across a repository "to find entities with a given name". Two unrelated functions with the same name in different modules will both show up. Check the file and its imports before you trust a reference.

blocks.question: You run `git grep -n parse_config` in a project and get no hits, but you can see `parse_config` in a file in your editor. Which explanation is most likely?
options: The file is untracked or ignored, and git grep searches tracked files only
git grep is case-insensitive by default
git grep needs `-r` to search subdirectories
git grep only searches the last commit, not the working tree
blocks.explain: By default git grep searches tracked files in the working tree. A new file you have not added, or one matched by .gitignore, is invisible to it. Use `--untracked` (and `--no-exclude-standard` for ignored files). Recursion is already the default, and the working tree, not HEAD, is searched.

blocks.question: Which GitHub code search query finds where Redis **defines** a function named lookupKeyRead?
blocks.explain: symbol: matches definitions and repo: scopes to one repository. repo: needs the full owner/name, since partial repository names are not supported. A bare term matches any file whose content or path contains it, so the first query returns every call site too.

lessons.title: Trace one request: a Redis GET from socket to reply

blocks.md: Now follow one feature end to end. A user reports that `GET` on a key holding a list replies `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`. We ran exactly that against a locally built server (`RPUSH l a`, then `GET l`) and got that reply. Where is it produced, and what path does a GET take to get there?

The usual first move is to search for the **observable string**: an error message, a log line or a URL. `git grep -n 'Operation against a key holding'` finds it in `src/server.c` inside `createSharedObjects`, stored as `shared.wrongtypeerr`, plus a constant in `redismodule.h` and five test assertions. Searching the variable, `git grep -w wrongtypeerr`, gives 7 lines; one of them is in `checkType` in `src/object.c`, which replies with that error when a key has the wrong type.

blocks.prompt: checkType is where the error comes from. Can you now walk upward through its callers to find the GET path?
blocks.reveal: Not efficiently. `git grep -w checkType` matches **122 lines in 15 files**: every command that checks a type calls it. Walking up from a widely shared helper fans out fast. Start from the specific end instead: the command. `src/commands/get.json` says `"function": "getCommand"`, and getCommand calls getGenericCommand, which calls checkType. Only 6 lines in the repo mention getGenericCommand.

blocks.md: So go **down** from the command. `git grep -n -w getCommand` returns just 4 lines: the JSON spec, the generated table in `src/commands.def`, a prototype in `src/server.h`, and the definition at `src/t_string.c:470`. There is **no call site**. Nothing in the code says `getCommand(c)`.

That is the signature of **dynamic dispatch**: the function is stored as a pointer in a table and called through the pointer. At startup `populateCommandTable` in `src/server.c` adds each entry of the generated table to a dictionary keyed by command name. For each request, the entry is found with `lookupCommand` (current Redis usually does this while parsing input, in `preprocessCommand`, and `processCommand` reuses the result), and `call` runs it with the line `c->cmd->proc(c);`. Text search cannot connect these: you find the table by searching the name, and the caller by searching the field (`git grep -n 'cmd->proc('`).

blocks.title: The path of GET through the Redis server

scenes.caption: When a client socket is readable, the event loop runs the read handler `readQueryFromClient`, which reads bytes into a buffer and calls `processInputBuffer` to parse complete commands.

For each parsed command, `processCommandAndResetClient` calls `processCommand`, which uses the entry `lookupCommand` found in the command table (simplified: recent Redis looks it up while parsing) and runs arity, ACL and other checks.
`call` invokes the looked-up entry through a function pointer: `c->cmd->proc(c)`. This dashed edge is the one grep cannot find, because no line names getCommand.
getCommand calls getGenericCommand, which looks the key up (db.c) and checks its type (object.c). For a list key, checkType sends the WRONGTYPE error.

blocks.title: getGenericCommand on GET l, where l holds a list

scenes.caption: Entry. `c->argv` holds the parsed arguments: argv[0] is GET and argv[1] is the key.
Look the key up. If it does not exist, lookupKeyReadOrReply sends the null reply itself and returns NULL, so GET returns early. Here l exists.
checkType compares the object's type with OBJ_STRING. A list does not match, so it sends shared.wrongtypeerr and returns 1.
scenes.output: -WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value

scenes.caption: getGenericCommand returns C_ERR. GET ignores the result; GETDEL and GETSET use it to stop before deleting or overwriting.

blocks.md: Reading the source gave us a path. You can also make the program **tell** you the path. A debugger breakpoint on `getCommand` followed by a backtrace does this; the GDB manual defines a backtrace as "a summary of how your program got where it is", one line per stack frame. Our sandbox did not allow attaching a debugger, so we added a temporary `backtrace_symbols_fd` call at the top of getCommand, rebuilt, and sent a GET.

blocks.code:
0   redis-server   getCommand + 52
1   redis-server   call + 624
2   redis-server   processCommand + 3992
3   redis-server   processInputBuffer + 5048
4   redis-server   readQueryFromClient + 1684
5   redis-server   connSocketEventHandler + 200
6   redis-server   aeProcessEvents + 1188
7   redis-server   main + 31588
blocks.caption: Real output (addresses removed) from the default optimized build on macOS. Frame 0 is the innermost call.

blocks.md: A backtrace from an optimized build can skip functions. The source says processInputBuffer calls processCommandAndResetClient, and main calls aeMain, which calls aeProcessEvents. Neither appears above: the compiler inlined them. Trust the source for the exact chain, and use the backtrace to confirm the route and catch dispatch that grep cannot see.

Trace from the specific end toward the general one. Start at the observable string or the command's own handler, search downward through callees, and use a backtrace (or a log line) to bridge function pointers, callbacks and event loops.

blocks.question: In a plugin-based web framework, `git grep -n -w handle_upload` finds only the definition and one line `routes = {"/upload": handle_upload}`. What is the best next search to find who runs it?
options: Conclude the function is dead code and propose deleting it
Search for `handle_upload(` with -w until a call appears
Search for where `routes` is read, for example `git grep -n -w routes`, to find the dispatcher that calls through the table
blocks.explain: A name stored in a table with no direct call is dynamic dispatch, as with Redis's command table. The caller looks up the table and calls the stored function, so search for the table's readers. Tests can help confirm behavior, but they do not show the production caller.

blocks.question: A backtrace shows `processInputBuffer` directly above `processCommand`, but the source shows processInputBuffer calls processCommandAndResetClient, which calls processCommand. What explains it?
options: The backtrace is from a different version of Redis
processCommandAndResetClient was inlined into its caller by the optimizing compiler, so it has no frame of its own
Backtraces only show functions defined in server.c
blocks.explain: Inlining copies a function's body into its caller, so no separate stack frame exists at run time. Debug builds without optimization keep more frames. The source code remains the ground truth for the call chain.

lessons.title: git blame: who last changed a line, and seeing past noise

blocks.md: You found the code. The next question a maintainer will ask is **why** it is written that way, because your patch may undo a deliberate decision. Version history answers it. To see each tool's exact behavior we built a small repository with four commits by four authors, all touching one file, `ratelimit.py`, a token-bucket rate limiter.

blocks.code:
git log --format='%h %an %ad %s' --date=short
7eb3ec2 dave 2024-07-15 Put allow() first, the public entry point
18f19b4 carol 2024-05-20 Style: switch to 2-space indentation
ebd5779 bob 2024-03-02 Raise BURST to 50: login bursts after deploys were hitting 429s
56dc3f4 alice 2024-01-10 Add token bucket rate limiter
blocks.caption: alice writes the file (RATE, BURST, refill, allow). bob changes one constant and explains why. carol only reindents. dave swaps the order of the two functions.

blocks.code:
RATE = 10    # tokens added per second
BURST = 50   # bucket capacity

def allow(bucket, now):
  refill(bucket, now)
  if bucket.tokens >= 1:
    bucket.tokens -= 1
    return True
  return False

def refill(bucket, now):
  elapsed = now - bucket.last
  bucket.tokens = min(BURST, bucket.tokens + elapsed * RATE)
  bucket.last = now
blocks.caption: The file today, 14 lines. Line 13 is the interesting one: who decided the bucket caps at BURST?

blocks.md: `git blame FILE` "annotates each line in the given file with information from the revision which last modified the line". The word **last** is the trap. A commit that only reindents or moves code becomes the last modifier of every line it touched, and hides the commit that actually wrote the logic. A `^` before a hash marks a boundary commit, here alice's root commit.

blocks.title: Author blamed for each of the 14 lines of ratelimit.py

scenes.caption: Plain `git blame`: carol's reindent owns allow's body (lines 5 to 9) and dave's move owns all of refill (10 to 14). Only 3 lines point to alice, who wrote nearly all of it.
`git blame -w` ignores whitespace when matching lines to the parent. allow's body goes back to alice, but refill still blames dave: a move is not a whitespace change.
`git blame -M` detects lines moved within the file. refill's header and the blank line go to alice, but its body shows carol, because the moved lines were also reindented.
`git blame -w -M` combines both: 13 lines blame alice and line 2 blames bob, who really changed BURST. Now line 13 points at the commit that wrote it.

blocks.md: Why did plain blame treat allow and refill differently? The git-blame manual describes it: when a commit swaps two blocks, "the traditional blame algorithm notices only half of the movement". It typically blames the block that moved **up** (allow) on the parent and the block that moved **down** (refill) on the moving commit. `-M` runs extra passes to blame both on the parent; it counts a move only when at least 20 alphanumeric characters match by default. `-C` also looks for lines moved or copied from other files modified in the same commit (default threshold 40).

blocks.prompt: Instead of `-w`, you run `git blame --ignore-rev 18f19b4 ratelimit.py`, ignoring carol's commit. Which lines change owner compared with plain blame?
blocks.reveal: Lines 5 to 9 go from carol to alice, exactly like `-w`, and refill (lines 10 to 14) still blames dave. `--ignore-rev` blames lines changed by the ignored commit "on the previous commit that changed that line or nearby lines". It does not detect moves, so dave's commit still needs `-M`.

blocks.md: Projects that run a formatter over the whole tree record those commits so nobody has to remember the hashes. The convention is a file named `.git-blame-ignore-revs` with one full commit hash per line and `#` comments. Locally, `git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs` applies it to every blame. GitHub's blame view applies the file automatically when it sits in the repository root.

blame only describes lines that exist now. The manual is explicit: the report does "not tell you anything about lines which have been deleted or replaced". If you want to know when a check was removed, blame cannot answer; the next lesson's pickaxe can.
blame follows whole-file renames automatically. For one region, `git blame -L 11,14 ratelimit.py` or `git blame -L :refill ratelimit.py` limits the output to a line range or a function.

blocks.question: Plain git blame says every line of a function was last changed by a commit titled "Run formatter". What is the most useful next command?
options: `git log -1` on that commit and conclude its author wrote the function
`git blame -w --ignore-rev <formatter-hash> file` to look past the formatting commit
blocks.explain: A formatting commit is the last modifier but not the author of the logic. Ignoring whitespace and the formatter commit points each line at the commit that changed its content. --reverse answers a different question: the last revision in which a line still existed.

blocks.question: A commit moved a 30-line function from the top of a file to the bottom, unchanged, past another function. Plain blame credits the moved lines to the move commit. Which option is designed for this?
blocks.explain: -M detects lines moved or copied within a file and blames them on the parent. -w only ignores whitespace differences, --first-parent changes how merges are walked, and -e shows email addresses instead of names.

lessons.title: Find the commit behind a change: log -S, -G and -L

blocks.md: blame starts from today's file. Often you need the opposite: start from a piece of code and find **the commit that introduced, changed or removed it**, including code that no longer exists. `git log` has three tools for this. The **pickaxe** options search inside each commit's diff: `-S<string>` and `-G<regex>`. The line-range option `-L` follows one region of one file back through history.

The definitions differ in one word. `-S<string>` looks for differences that "change the number of occurrences" of the string in a file. `-G<regex>` looks for differences whose patch text "contains added/removed lines that match" the regex. A commit that edits a line but keeps the string's count the same is invisible to -S and visible to -G.

blocks.prompt: In our ratelimit.py repository, bob changed `BURST = 20` to `BURST = 50`. Which commits does `git log -S BURST` list?
blocks.reveal: Only **alice's** commit. She took BURST from 0 occurrences to 2 (the constant and its use in refill). bob's commit removed one line containing BURST and added another, so the count stayed at 2 and -S skips it. To find bob's change with -S you must search for text whose count changed: `git log -S'BURST = 50'` lists exactly bob's commit.

blocks.title: Which commits each history query lists

scenes.caption: `git log -S BURST`: only alice, who changed how many times BURST occurs. bob's edit and the moves keep the count at 2.
`git log -S'BURST = 50'`: only bob, the commit where that exact text first appears.
`git log -G BURST`: all four. carol's reindent and dave's move both remove and re-add the line using BURST in refill, and -G matches any added or removed line.
`git log -L :allow:ratelimit.py` follows the allow function: alice wrote it, carol reindented it, dave's commit added a blank line at its end.
`git log -L :refill:ratelimit.py` lists only dave. His diff shows refill deleted at the top and added at the bottom, so the traced range starts in his commit.
Restart -L just before the move: `git log -L :refill:ratelimit.py 7eb3ec2^` lists carol and alice. Feeding the pre-move version back in recovers the full history.

blocks.md: So -S is precise (it lists the commits that added or removed the text, usually what you want for "when did this call appear?" or "when was this check deleted?") and -G is broad (any commit that touched a matching line). The docs give an example where `-G"frotz\(nitfol"` shows a commit but the equivalent `-S` does not, because the number of occurrences did not change.

blocks.code:
git log -L :refill:ratelimit.py --no-patch --oneline
7eb3ec2 Put allow() first, the public entry point

git log -L :refill:ratelimit.py --no-patch --oneline 7eb3ec2^
18f19b4 Style: switch to 2-space indentation
56dc3f4 Add token bucket rate limiter

git log -S'elapsed = now - bucket.last' --oneline
56dc3f4 Add token bucket rate limiter
blocks.caption: Real output from our repository. -L stops at a move; restarting it from the parent of the move commit, or a -S search for a line inside the block, gets past it.

blocks.md: `-L` takes either `<start>,<end>:<file>` (line numbers or regexes) or `:<funcname>:<file>`, where funcname is a regex for the function header line, found with the same hunk-header rules as git grep -p. It walks history from one starting revision and prints the patch for that range in every commit that touched it. The git-log manual recommends using -S iteratively in the same spirit: find the commit, take the older version of the block from its diff, and search again until you reach the first version.

Once you have the commit, read it whole: `git show ebd5779` prints the message and diff. bob's message carries the reason, "login bursts after deploys were hitting 429s". If the project merges through pull requests, the review discussion around that commit often explains even more. That is the context a maintainer expects you to have read before proposing `BURST = 20` again.

Pick the tool by question. Who last touched this line: `git blame -w -M`. When did this text appear or disappear: `git log -S'text'`. Which commits touched lines matching a pattern: `git log -G'regex'`. How did this function evolve: `git log -L :func:file`. Then read the commit message and its pull request.

`git log --follow -- path` continues a single file's history past renames. Combine pickaxe options with a pathspec, for example `git log -S'checkType' -- src/t_string.c`, to keep a search over a big history fast and focused.

blocks.question: A security check `if (!is_admin(user))` used to exist in auth.c and is gone today. Which command finds the commit that deleted it?
options: `git log --follow auth.c` and read every diff
blocks.explain: Deleting the check lowers the number of occurrences of that text, which is exactly what -S finds. blame and grep only see lines that exist now. Reading every diff works but is what the pickaxe automates.

blocks.question: A commit changed `timeout = 30` to `timeout = 60` on the same line. Which search lists that commit?
blocks.explain: The count of "timeout" did not change (one line removed, one added), so -S skips the commit. -G matches the removed and the added line, so it lists it. `git log -S'timeout = 60'` would also work because that exact text went from 0 to 1 occurrence.
